meta.description: Real Dostoevsky — but the famous English wording is Andrew MacAndrew's 1970 translation, and the Grand Inquisitor says it, not the novelist.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The mystery of human existence lies not in just staying alive, but in finding something to live for'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Dostoevsky, from The Brothers Karamazov. The catch: this exact phrasing is a 1970 translator's, and the speaker is a character.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1821–1881 · Russian novelist — spoken by the Grand Inquisitor in his final novel
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. The sentence is from The Brothers Karamazov (serialised 1879–80), Book V, chapter 5, “The Grand Inquisitor” — the Russian original reads “Ибо тайна бытия человеческого не в том, чтобы только жить, а в том, для чего жить”. Two caveats worth knowing: this exact English phrasing is Andrew R. MacAndrew’s 1970 translation ↗, not Dostoevsky’s words in English, and the speaker is a character — the Inquisitor, not the novelist.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Book V, “Pro and Contra,” chapter 5: “The Grand Inquisitor”
Serialised in The Russian Messenger, January 1879 – November 1880; book edition 1880
Andrew R. MacAndrew, 1970 (Bantam Books, New York)

source.excerpt: This is something about which You were right. For the mystery of human existence lies not in just staying alive, but in finding something to live for. Without a concrete idea of what he is living for, man would refuse to live, would rather exterminate himself than remain on this earth, even if bread were scattered all around him.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes this exact English wording from Andrew MacAndrew’s Bantam translation of The Brothers Karamazov, Book V ch. 5, and concludes that Dostoevsky should receive credit for the quotation.
The Russian original is there in the chapter itself: Russian Wikisource ↗ carries “Ибо тайна бытия человеческого не в том, чтобы только жить, а в том, для чего жить” in the Grand Inquisitor’s speech.

We checked the wording against Constance Garnett’s English: her translation at Project Gutenberg ↗ reads “For the secret of man’s being is not only to live but to have something to live for” — a different sentence, which is why the Garnett credit some quote sites attach to this wording does not hold.
Wikipedia ↗ dates Andrew R. MacAndrew’s translation to 1970 and the novel’s serialisation to January 1879 – November 1880; an Internet Archive catalogue record ↗ lists a 1970 edition credited to him.
source.excerptNote: MacAndrew’s English, as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. The speaker is the Grand Inquisitor, addressing a silent Christ; the Russian original runs “Ибо тайна бытия человеческого не в том, чтобы только жить, а в том, для чего жить.”

source.rightsNote: Dostoevsky’s Russian original (1879–80) is long in the public domain, and so is Constance Garnett’s 1912 English translation. But the wording quoted here is not either of those — it is Andrew R. MacAndrew’s 1970 translation for Bantam Books, and a 1970 translation is a protected work in the United States. Treat this exact English sentence as in copyright; if you need a free-to-reuse rendering, use Garnett’s public-domain text ↗ instead.

author.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
author.heading: Who was Fyodor Dostoevsky?
author.bio: Dostoevsky was a Russian novelist, short-story writer, essayist and journalist whose fiction turned interrogation rooms, gambling dens and monastery cells into laboratories for questions about freedom, guilt and belief. Crime and Punishment (1866), The Idiot (1869) and Demons (1872) made his name; The Brothers Karamazov, serialised in The Russian Messenger from January 1879 to November 1880, was his last novel. He died in Saint Petersburg on 9 February 1881, a few months after finishing it.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong about it
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Dostoevsky holds up — unusually, for a line this widely posted. What goes wrong is downstream: which Englishing it is, who in the book is speaking, and what the sentence is doing there.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ prints this exact wording under The Brothers Karamazov, Book V ch. 5, labelled “trans. Constance Garnett.” Garnett’s text says something else: her translation at Project Gutenberg ↗ reads “For the secret of man’s being is not only to live but to have something to live for.” Quote Investigator ↗ traces the “mystery of human existence” phrasing to Andrew MacAndrew’s Bantam translation instead.

Quote Investigator ↗ notes the saying appears as dialogue, spoken by the Grand Inquisitor character. It sits two layers deep: the Inquisitor is a figure in a poem Ivan Karamazov recites to his brother Alyosha, and Ivan is not Dostoevsky either.

In the novel the sentence is part of an argument for taking freedom away, not for finding your calling. The surrounding passage ↗ has the Inquisitor telling a silent Christ that whoever masters a man’s conscience owns him, and that bread alone will not keep people alive.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Dostoevsky’s, written in Russian for The Brothers Karamazov in 1879–80. The famous English sentence is translator Andrew MacAndrew’s, and the mouth it comes out of belongs to the Grand Inquisitor — as Quote Investigator documents ↗.

context.heading: What the Inquisitor is actually arguing
lead: Pulled out on its own, the line sounds like a motivational poster. In the novel it is the opposite of encouragement. Ivan Karamazov is reciting a “poem” to his brother Alyosha in which a cardinal of the Spanish Inquisition arrests a silent Christ and lectures him on where he went wrong: people cannot bear freedom, they want bread and certainty, and the Church has quietly relieved them of the burden of choosing.

The famous sentence is a step in that prosecution. Right before it the Inquisitor says that whoever captures a man’s conscience owns him; right after it he adds that without a settled idea of what he is living for, a man “would refuse to live, would rather exterminate himself than remain on this earth, even if bread were scattered all around him.” The need for something to live for is offered as leverage — the lever the Inquisitor uses to justify taking freedom away.
context.detailsSummary: Why the English wording varies so much
detailsBody: Dostoevsky wrote one Russian sentence; English has produced many. Constance Garnett’s 1912 version renders it “For the secret of man’s being is not only to live but to have something to live for.” MacAndrew’s 1970 version reads “For the mystery of human existence lies not in just staying alive, but in finding something to live for.” Both are translating тайна бытия человеческого — literally the mystery or secret of human being.
The version that went viral online is MacAndrew’s, which is why quote sites that credit the sentence to a different translator are quietly wrong even when the attribution to Dostoevsky is right.
context.pull: It is not advice about how to live. It is an argument for why people will trade their freedom to be told.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes Dostoevsky should receive credit for this quotation, which appeared in The Brothers Karamazov, and transcribes the exact wording "For the mystery of human existence lies not in just staying alive, but in finding something to live for" from Andrew MacAndrew's translation, Book V ch. 5 (The Grand Inquisitor), Bantam Books, New York — noting the words are dialogue spoken by the Grand Inquisitor character.

Quote Investigator gives Constance Garnett's 1912 rendering as "For the secret of man's being is not only to live but to have something to live for" (William Heinemann, London, page 268), and notes Max Tegmark used this saying as a chapter epigraph in Life 3.0 (2017).

Constance Garnett's English translation of The Brothers Karamazov reads "For the secret of man's being is not only to live but to have something to live for. Without a stable conception of the object of life, man would not consent to go on living..." and does not contain the phrase "mystery of human existence". Verified by full-text grep of the Project Gutenberg file (eBook #28054, Translator: Constance Garnett).
The Russian original in Братья Карамазовы, Книга пятая, V reads "Ибо тайна бытия человеческого не в том, чтобы только жить, а в том, для чего жить." within the Grand Inquisitor's speech.

Wikiquote's Fyodor Dostoyevsky page lists "For the mystery of human existence lies not in just staying alive but in finding something to live for." under The Brothers Karamazov (1879–1880) with the sub-line "Book V, ch. 5 (trans. Constance Garnett)". Verified against the raw wikitext.

The Brothers Karamazov was serialised in The Russian Messenger from January 1879 to November 1880 and published as a separate edition in 1880; the list of notable English translations includes Andrew R. MacAndrew (1970).

Fyodor Dostoevsky was born 11 November 1821 in Moscow and died 9 February 1881 in Saint Petersburg; he was a Russian novelist, short-story writer, essayist and journalist, and The Brothers Karamazov was his final novel.
Internet Archive holds a catalogue record for The Brothers Karamazov dated 1970 with creator "Andrew R. MacAndrew" (identifier bwb_S0-BLA-666).
